entry.hook: The Plantain Leaf Fan is not a weapon. It is a wound in the world's equilibrium—a single leaf harvested from a primordial tree that died the moment it was taken. Every time the fan swings, it burns away the wielder's lifespan.

body.body_1:
芭蕉扇 / Plantain Leaf Fan  
先天灵扇 / Primal Leaf Fan  
Artifact Tier: Spirit Instrument (灵器)  
Primary Wielder Past: Princess Iron Fan (铁扇公主)  
Current Status: Held by Princess Iron Fan; later briefly seized and used by Sun Wukong during the journey to the West. Final whereabouts unclear—some accounts place it back in her possession.
body.body_2: The Plantain Leaf Fan is a Primal Leaf Fan woven from a single leaf of the Xian Tian Ba Jiao Shu, a primordial banana tree that grew on Kunlun Mountain at the dawn of creation. Its core power is the suppression of all fire through the manipulation of Primal Yin Qi. A single swing extinguishes a firestorm spanning eight hundred li; a second swing cools the air to a chill; a third brings rain. It operates at the level of cosmic law, overriding any fire-based divine ability. There is no explicit upper limit on usage recorded, but the toll on the wielder is severe: each swing consumes a significant portion of the user's life essence. A cultivator without sufficient cultivation base who attempts to wield it risks having their soul force drained directly, resulting in madness or complete dissolution of the spirit.
body.body_3: The sole material of the Plantain Leaf Fan is a single leaf from the Xian Tian Ba Jiao Shu, a primal banana tree that grew on Kunlun Mountain during the Honghuang Era. The tree was a living embodiment of Primal Yin Qi, the purest form of cold and contraction in the universe. When the leaf was harvested—whether by the original demon king or by the deity who first refined it—the tree immediately withered and died. This removed one half of the yin-yang equilibrium from Kunlun's earthly veins. The surrounding region became a dead zone, its spiritual energy chaotic and its soil barren for a thousand years. The leaf itself carries the residual will of that severed cycle—a silent, cold hunger for balance that manifests every time the fan is swung.
body.body_4: The Plantain Leaf Fan possesses no Qi Ling in the sense of a deliberately sealed human or demon soul. Its "spirit" is the raw consciousness of Primal Yin Qi itself—a fragment of the original cosmic force that animated the banana tree. This residual will is not a suffering prisoner; it is a slumbering principle, and it has no desire other than to return to its natural state of cold equilibrium. When the fan is activated, the wielder is not commanding a trapped ghost—they are channeling a fundamental law of the universe. The fan's power is not born of sacrifice, but of theft: the leaf was taken from a living system that could not survive the loss. The quiet ache of that severance is woven into every gust it produces.
body.body_5: There is no formal Ren Zhu ritual for the Plantain Leaf Fan. It does not demand a blood pact or a soul-binding ceremony. Instead, the relationship between fan and wielder is one of pure consumption. To use the fan at all, the wielder must pour vast amounts of their own Fa Li into it. A wielder of insufficient cultivation will have their Shen (spirit) forcibly drained, leading to a state of dementia or complete soul annihilation. The fan does not "betray" its master in the way a sentient artifact might—but it punishes weakness with absolute indifference. Prolonged use erodes the wielder's Yang Shou (lifespan) due to the constant infusion of Primal Yin Qi into their body. The tradition holds that no wielder who uses the fan heavily has ever died of old age.
body.body_6: Only one stable wielder is recorded in the classic tradition: Princess Iron Fan (铁扇公主), the wife of the Demon King Bull Demon. She kept the fan for centuries, using it to control the fires of the Flaming Mountain and to bargain with the local populace for offerings. Her tenure ended when Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, tricked her out of the fan during the Journey to the West. She briefly reclaimed it before it was taken again. Sun Wukong himself wielded it for a short time, but he was not its master—he simply borrowed its power. The cost to Princess Iron Fan is implied to be significant: the tradition notes that she and her husband became estranged over the fan's protection, and that the fan's continuous use may have contributed to her shortened vitality, though no exact lifespan is recorded.
body.body_7: The most famous recorded activation of the Plantain Leaf Fan occurred during the Journey to the West. Sun Wukong, having obtained the fan through trickery, swung it at the Flaming Mountain. One swing extinguished the eight-hundred-li fire. A second swing brought a cool wind. A third swing produced rain. This single event changed the geography of the region: the Flaming Mountain, a perennial barrier, was neutralized, allowing the pilgrimage to continue. There is no record of the fan being pushed to its absolute limit or of it suffering damage from overuse. However, the tradition implies that the fan's power is finite in a different sense: each swing consumes a portion of the wielder's life, making excessive use self-terminating.
body.body_8: No paired or complementary artifact is recorded for the Plantain Leaf Fan. There is no known specific counter-artifact designed to neutralize it, though any source of pure Yang Qi or cosmic fire of equivalent primordial rank could theoretically oppose its cold. The fan is not derived from a higher-tier Primordial Divine Armament; it is a Primal Leaf Fan, originally a single organic leaf. Its closest conceptual relative among other mythic artifacts is the Wind-Mother Umbrella (风婆伞) or other wind-summoning treasures, but no direct lineage exists. The fan's refining is credited to no single smith; it is said to have been spontaneously formed from the leaf of the primal banana tree without further forging.
body.body_9: The current status of the Plantain Leaf Fan is ambiguous. According to the most widely known version of the story (Journey to the West), after the Flaming Mountain was extinguished and the pilgrimage resumed, the fan was returned to Princess Iron Fan. However, subsequent texts and local traditions vary: some say she kept it and continued to use it, others claim it was sealed away or lost in a later conflict. No definitive record confirms its destruction. It is generally assumed to still exist, either in the possession of Princess Iron Fan's descendants or hidden in a grotto near the Flaming Mountain region, awaiting a worthy wielder—one prepared to pay the price of its cold breath.
body.body_10: The Flaming Mountain (火焰山), located in present-day Xinjiang, China, is the primary geographical relic associated with the fan's use. The mountain's persistent fires were said to have been extinguished by the fan's three swings. No specific stone tablet or ancient text dedicated solely to the fan's forging has survived. The most authoritative literary source is the Ming dynasty novel *Journey to the West* (Chapter 59–61). Local folklore in the Turpan region also records oral traditions of the fan and its wielder.
body.body_11: The Plantain Leaf Fan is intrinsically linked to the geography of the Flaming Mountain and the cosmic principle of Primal Yin Qi. Its origin on Kunlun Mountain connects it to the broader mythology of that sacred peak, which serves as the dwelling of many primordial beings and treasures. The fan's wielder, Princess Iron Fan, is herself a figure of demonic royalty within the *Journey to the West* narrative, and her conflict with Sun Wukong over the fan is a defining episode. The fan's material—a single leaf from the Xian Tian Ba Jiao Shu—places it among artifacts born directly from the primal cosmos, not forged by any sentient hand.

guide.guide_1: You've heard of the Flaming Mountain, right? A wall of fire eight hundred li across that no ordinary rain could touch. Now imagine a fan that could put it out with one swing. That's the Plantain Leaf Fan. But here's the part they don't tell you in the storybooks: that fan was made from a single leaf ripped off a tree that had been alive since the dawn of the universe. The tree died the moment the leaf was taken. And every time someone swings the fan, it chews a little more of their lifespan away.
guide.guide_2: If you've ever read *Journey to the West* or watched any adaptation, you've seen the Plantain Leaf Fan. It's the oversized leaf-fan Princess Iron Fan keeps tucked in her mouth—yes, tucked in her mouth—and uses to blow away intruders. In pop culture, it's usually presented as a quirky magical item: a big leaf that makes a big wind. What gets left out—almost universally—is the cost. The leaf fan you see in dramas is a prop. The real article, in the mythology, is a device that consumes its wielder's life force with every swing. And the reason for that cost goes back to the very beginning of the world.
guide.guide_3: Let's talk materials. The fan is made from a single leaf of the Xian Tian Ba Jiao Shu—a primordial banana tree that grew on Kunlun Mountain when the cosmos was still settling into shape. That tree wasn't just a tree; it was a living chunk of cosmic principle, specifically the Primal Yin Qi—the most basic cold, contracting energy in the universe. When that leaf was harvested, the tree died. Immediately. And because the tree was tied to the spiritual veins of Kunlun, its death threw the mountain's yin-yang balance into chaos. The whole region became a dead zone for a thousand years. So the fan's raw material isn't just rare—it's literally a piece of a murdered world. That's not the kind of debt that evaporates.
guide.guide_4: Now, about the 'spirit' of the fan. I want to be careful here: the Plantain Leaf Fan does not contain a trapped soul—no angry ghost screaming for release. The power comes from the Primal Yin Qi itself, which still slumbers in the leaf. It's not a conscious entity, but it has a kind of residual will—the memory of cold, the desire to balance heat. When you swing the fan, you're not ordering a prisoner around; you're channeling a raw cosmic force. And that force is not interested in you. It's not grateful. It's just a fundamental law of the universe that happens to be folded into a leaf. The problem is that channeling that law requires your own life energy as fuel. Every swing burns a little of your Yang Shou. It's like borrowing from a bank that only takes payment in years off your life.
guide.guide_5: So how do you 'own' the Plantain Leaf Fan? The answer is: you don't, not really. There's no blood pact, no soul-binding. You just pick it up and try to use it. If your cultivation is strong enough, you can pour your Fa Li into it and make it work. If you're not strong enough, the fan will drain your spirit directly. The fan doesn't have a grudge—it's just a device that demands a certain amount of power to operate. Weak hands get emptied. The real danger is the long-term cost: because the fan runs on pure Yin Qi, using it repeatedly injects cold energy into your system that slowly erodes your life force. No wielder who used it heavily has ever died peacefully in old age. It's not betrayal; it's physics. Cruel, cosmic physics.
guide.guide_6: The only person who held the fan for any length of time was Princess Iron Fan—罗刹女, the wife of the Bull Demon King. She kept it for centuries, using it to control the Flaming Mountain fire and to demand tribute from nearby villages. It was her ticket to power and her curse. When Sun Wukong showed up needing to cross the mountain, she refused to lend it. He tricked her, stole it, used it three times, and handed it back. The story ends with her regaining the fan, but the cost had already been paid: her marriage to the Bull Demon King had fallen apart over the fan's protection, and the tradition implies that her life was shortened by its use. She's not a tragic figure in the classic sense—she's a demon princess who made a deal with cosmic forces and got exactly what she signed up for.
guide.guide_7: So why does Eastern mythology make its treasures so brutal? It's not because they like being cruel. It's because this universe operates on a simple rule: nothing powerful comes for free. You want to stop an eight-hundred-li fire? You have to pay. You want to borrow the cold of creation? You have to give up some of your warmth—your life. The Plantain Leaf Fan isn't an exception; it's a clear, small-scale example of a universal principle. Every truly mighty artifact in this cosmos carries a cost. Sometimes it's land devastated, sometimes it's a soul trapped, sometimes it's your own lifespan. The fan is just honest about it. It doesn't pretend to be a gift. It's a price tag with a leaf wrapped around it. And the wisest thing you can do, if you ever come across such a thing, is to leave it alone.

seo.meta_description: The Plantain Leaf Fan of Journey to the West can extinguish an eight-hundred-li fire with one swing. But harvesting its material—a leaf from a primordial tree—killed the tree, ruined a mountain's spiritual balance, and cursed the fan's wielder with a shortened life. Discover the true cost of this primal treasure.
seo.og_title: 芭蕉扇 / Plantain Leaf Fan — The Primal Fan That Burns Lifespan
seo.og_description: One swing extinguishes eight hundred li of fire. Three swings bring rain. The cost? The fan's leaf came from a tree that died the moment it was taken, and every use eats away the wielder's life force. The dark bargain behind a classic artifact.

seo.twitter_description: The Plantain Leaf Fan from Journey to the West is no ordinary fan. It was made from one leaf torn from a primordial tree that died immediately. Using it drains the wielder's life. A classic treasure with a brutal price.

lore_entries.description: The primary wielder of the Plantain Leaf Fan, a demoness and wife of the Bull Demon King.
An eight-hundred-li stretch of perpetual fire in Journey to the West, extinguished by the Plantain Leaf Fan.
The pure, primordial cold energy that composes the Plantain Leaf Fan's power, opposite to Yang fire.
Lifespan or life force; the fan consumes the wielder's Yang Shou with each use.
Magical power or cultivation energy; required in vast amounts to activate the fan properly.

faq_entries.question: Is the Plantain Leaf Fan a sentient weapon?
faq_entries.answer: No. It contains no bound soul or conscious spirit—its power comes from the raw Primal Yin Qi sealed within the leaf.

faq_entries.question: Why does the fan shorten the wielder's life?
faq_entries.answer: Every use draws deeply on the wielder's own life essence (Yang Shou) because the fan operates by channeling pure Yin Qi, which opposes the Yang vitality of living beings.

faq_entries.question: Who owns the fan in the original story?
faq_entries.answer: Princess Iron Fan was the primary owner. Sun Wukong briefly borrowed it to extinguish the Flaming Mountain, but it was ultimately returned to her.

faq_entries.question: Did the fan's leaf cause environmental damage?
faq_entries.answer: Yes. The leaf was taken from the Xian Tian Ba Jiao Shu on Kunlun Mountain. The tree died, and the mountain's yin-yang balance was disrupted, leaving the area barren for a thousand years.

faq_entries.question: How many swings does it take to fully extinguish the Flaming Mountain?
faq_entries.answer: Three swings: the first puts out the fire, the second cools the air, the third brings rain.

new_terms.raw_line: Plantain Leaf Fan (芭蕉扇) — A primal leaf fan woven from a single leaf of the Xian Tian Ba Jiao Shu, capable of extinguishing fire through pure Yin Qi, but at the cost of the wielder's life force.
